newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Petronas seen gaining from Malaysian ringgit fall.
newsitem.headline: Petronas seen gaining from Malaysian ringgit fall.

text.p: Malaysia's state-oil company Petronas will not be adversely affected by a significant weakening of the ringgit, company officials and analysts said on Thursday.
As a net exporter of crude and oil products, Petronas generates most sales in dollars, so, if anything, the company would benefit from a fall in the ringgit.
Oil companies in the Philippines and Thailand have been tipped by analysts to expect a rough time in the wake of the effective devaluation of the peso and the baht.
Shares in Philippines state-refiner Petron have fallen sharply and analysts forecast the company will have to raise domestic oil prices to offset the increase in import costs.
Oil companies in Thailand have already started raising prices to recoup the squeeze on their margins.
The devaluations sparked a sell off of South East Asian currencies.
The ringgit was not unscathed and this week fell as low as 2.59 to the dollar -- the lowest level since July 1994.
But analysts were sanguine about Petronas prospects.
"Most of Petronas' costs are in ringgit while its sales are in dollars," said an analyst with European financial house in Kuala Lumpur.
He said crude prices are expected to fall this year, but the decline in the ringgit will help to offset that because the currency translation favours the dollar.
Another analyst agreed and said the detrimental affect of a weaker ringgit on Petronas would be more than offset by the benefits derived from its dollar sales.
Malaysia is one of the largest crude producers in Asia with daily output of around 655,000 barrels-per-day.
Petronas owns 60 percent of the offtake, the rest goes to affiliates. Malaysian crude exports were running at 375,000 bpd at the end of last year.
It also has five refineries, which all run Malaysian crude, with output capacity of mroe than 470,000 bpd.
Petronas also exports jet fuel, naphtha and low sulphur waxy residue and imports a small volume of fuel oil.
Petronas has operated a policy in recent years of expanding internationally in both upstream and downstream operations, which analysts said meant more of the company was dollar based.
It plans to generate one-third of its consolidated turnover from operations outside Malaysia by 2005.
Sharp crude prices gains in 1996 were largely behind the company's 44.7 percent rise in pretax profits to 12.39 billion ringgit ($4.88 billion) in the year ended March 31.
Sales rose 30 percent to 28.89 billion ringgit and two-third were derived from crude and oil products exports -- a dollar-based market.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3086)
